before: You ride from school to home. Build a model that predicts how long the ride will take.
after: With your teacher, mark a safe, unobstructed 10 m corridor. One learner walks normally while a partner times the walk. Repeat three times and record each time.

before: Write two lists: what your model keeps, and what it leaves out. Then swap lists with somebody who takes a different route home and argue about the differences. Finally, say what your model would get badly wrong — every model has an answer to that.
after: Use the measured average time to predict a 20 m walk at the same pace. Test that prediction. What changes if the walker starts from rest, turns a corner or changes speed? Keep observations separate from explanations.

before: Not because it stands for anything in English. The symbol comes from the Latin celeritas , meaning swiftness, and it stuck through habit and agreement rather than logic — as a good many symbols have.
after: The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299 792 458 metres per second in SI. Its fixed value helps define the metre. Measurements still test instruments and physical models, but the numerical value of this defining constant is not an experimental uncertainty.

before: In everyday speech, it's only a theory means it is a guess somebody has not bothered to check. In science the word means close to the opposite. A theory is what an idea is promoted to after it has survived a great deal of checking, made predictions that came true, and explained things it was not invented to explain.
after: In everyday speech, theory can mean an untested guess. A scientific theory is a broad explanatory framework assessed against evidence. It makes predictions and connects observations; the label does not make it immune to revision.

before: Nothing arrives as a theory. Ideas start as hunches, become hypotheses that can be tested, and are called theories only once the evidence is substantial. Calling something a theory in this book is a statement of confidence, not a hedge.
after: A hypothesis is a testable proposed explanation. A theory is not a hypothesis promoted after a fixed number of successful tests, and a theory does not become a law. The terms describe different roles, not ranks of certainty.

before: Suppose, to keep it simple, that all their food is rice. An adult needs roughly 2000 to 2500 kilocalories a day, and 100 g of uncooked rice provides about 350 of them. So one adult needs about $2000 \div 350 \approx 6$ hundred-gram portions — call it 600 g of rice a day.
after: For an energy-equivalent estimate, assume four adults each need 2100 kilocalories daily and uncooked rice supplies 350 kilocalories per 100 g. That gives 600 g per adult daily, or about 72 kg for four adults over 30 days. These are stated model assumptions, not a diet recommendation.
